title: A24's 'Tony' Biopic Captures Anthony Bourdain as a Restless 19-Year-Old Before Fame
excerpt: Directed by Matt Johnson and starring Dominic Sessa, the coming-of-age film explores the summer of 1975 that steered Bourdain toward kitchens — and away from a life of bluffing.
body:
• A24's Tony, directed by Matt Johnson and starring Dominic Sessa, focuses on a single transformative summer in 1975 when a 19-year-old Anthony Bourdain stumbled into a Provincetown kitchen and discovered his calling.
  • Antonio Banderas plays the rigorous head chef, Eric Ripert appears in a cameo, and Bourdain's estate — through literary agent Kimberly Witherspoon — has endorsed the project.
  • The film arrives in U.S. cinemas in August 2026, offering a coming-of-age portrait rather than a conventional cradle-to-grave biopic.

A Summer That Changed Everything

The Anthony Bourdain who appears in A24's Tony is not the globe-trotting CNN host or the swaggering author of Kitchen Confidential. He is a 19-year-old punk from New Jersey who has just lost a writing fellowship he bragged about to everyone, and who follows a girl — loosely based on his first wife, Nancy Putkoski — to Provincetown, Massachusetts, in the summer of 1975.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=k1MVnzd2aVc

There, played by Dominic Sessa of The Holdovers, young Tony fibs about his qualifications, talks his way into a restaurant kitchen, and finds himself entranced by its intoxicating mix of chaos and discipline. By the film's final scene, he has decided to apply to the Culinary Institute of America — the first concrete step in a career that would reshape how millions think about food, travel, and storytelling.

A Deliberate Departure from Convention

Director Matt Johnson, best known for BlackBerry, has crafted what he calls a film "for people who had no idea who Anthony Bourdain was." Co-writers Todd Bartels and Lou Howe deliberately avoided the standard biopic structure, describing themselves as "allergic" to movies that compress a life into two hours.

https://x.com/WSJ/status/2083380961648206312

"We wanted to go back to the beginning, instead of the end, when his life was messy. He said he treated the world like his ashtray, but, ultimately, it was all potential and hope and promise."

— Todd Bartels, Co-writer

The screenplay draws from a section of Kitchen Confidential, Laurie Woolever's 2021 oral biography Bourdain: The Definitive Oral Biography, and the Massachusetts episode of Parts Unknown where Bourdain revisited Provincetown. The filmmakers leaned into the gaps in the historical record, using Bourdain's own tendency for "writerly flare" as licence to invent composite characters, including those played by Antonio Banderas and Leo Woodall.

Banderas portrays the kitchen's fastidious head chef — a disciplinarian who represents the ethical rigour Bourdain would later embody on screen. Woodall plays Sal, a drug-addled wild card who embodies the "libertine" side of restaurant culture that Bourdain documented throughout his career.

Estate Backing and a Symbolic Cameo

The film carries an unusual stamp of legitimacy. Kimberly Witherspoon, Bourdain's former literary agent who now oversees his estate, serves as executive producer. In a statement, the estate said it supported Tony because it "is not a standard biopic and doesn't attempt to summarize a life," calling the film "an interpretation" that captures Bourdain's "complexity, his intellectual appetite and his conviction."

Michelin-starred chef Eric Ripert, one of Bourdain's closest friends, appears in a cameo as a Culinary Institute interviewer. Looking at Tony's thin resume, Ripert's character delivers the film's thematic punchline: "At least he's honest."

"What transforms Anthony Bourdain the boy into Anthony Bourdain the man is that he no longer feels like he needs to lie to inflate his status."

— Matt Johnson, Director

Ripert, who agreed to the role without reading the script based on his trust in Witherspoon, acknowledged that the film's young Bourdain is nothing like the friend he knew. "Anthony in the movie lies a lot," Ripert said. "I never saw Anthony lying during all the years that we were together as friends."

Why This Film Resonates With Indian Audiences

Few Western media figures engaged with India as honestly as Bourdain did. His Parts Unknown episode on Punjab — where he visited Amritsar's dhabas, sat cross-legged at a gurdwara langar, and explored the region's history of resilience — remains one of the show's most celebrated hours. It was there that the famously anti-vegetarian chef admitted that Indian food was "the only place on earth" where he could eat vegetarian happily. "The food is so proudly prepared; the textures are very colorful and spicy," he told CNN.

His travels through Kerala's backwaters, Mumbai's Bhendi Bazaar, and Kolkata's street food circuits went beyond culinary tourism. As the Indian publication Homegrown noted in a recent essay timed to the Tony trailer, Bourdain "never claimed expertise" about India and "seemed to humble him." He once described the country as "a life's work — and an unfinished one — no matter how long we spent there."

For the Indian diaspora, Bourdain's legacy runs deeper than television ratings. He brought dhabas, langars, and sadhya meals to mainstream American screens at a time when Indian cuisine was largely reduced to tikka masala stereotypes, helping normalize a richer, more textured understanding of the subcontinent's food cultures.

What's Next

Tony opens in U.S. cinemas in August 2026. The cast also includes Emilia Jones, Dagmara Dominczyk, Rich Sommer, and Stavros Halkias. International release dates have not been confirmed, but A24's growing global distribution — including strong theatrical presence in India — suggests the film will reach South Asian audiences before the end of the year.

The film wisely avoids the "cottage industry" that co-writer Bartels says grew around Bourdain's death, including the controversial 2021 documentary Roadrunner. Instead, it bets that audiences will connect with a simpler story: a young man who lied his way into a kitchen and, in the heat and noise, finally found a reason to be honest.
nri_angle: Bourdain's deep engagement with India — from Punjab's langars to Kerala's backwaters — challenged Western stereotypes about Indian cuisine and brought dhabas and sadhya meals to mainstream American audiences.
